name: Indie Game Project Pitch Deck
description: A cinematic dark pitch system for making an indie game's fantasy, core loop, audience, production evidence, business model, roadmap, budget, and partner ask legible to investors and publishers.
style_guide:
# Indie Game Project Pitch Deck

## Design intent

Create a compelling but production-aware pitch for an independent PC, console, or cross-platform game. The visual language combines a dark editorial interface with hand-painted world art: near-black blue canvases, warm ember orange for fantasy and funding emphasis, mint green for loops and verified progress, warm-white type, cinematic key art, and compact production evidence.

The deck should make the player's fantasy, moment-to-moment loop, aesthetic, audience, differentiation, current build, commercial plan, team capability, schedule, budget, and partner need inspectable. The reference previews are visual-language examples only. Do not copy their studio, game title, world, characters, mechanics, art, player personas, market data, wishlists, pricing, team, roadmap, budget, raise, or release date.

## Canvas and grid

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas with `32–42 px` side margins, a `24–32 px` project header, and a `20–26 px` footer for version, source, or build status.
- Use a 12-column grid with `14–18 px` gutters. Align concept panels, loop stages, comparison rows, art crops, player profiles, evidence cards, revenue tables, timelines, budget bands, and team columns.
- Reserve `85–120 px` for a section code, conclusion-first headline, and concise setup. Let one gameplay, world, or production exhibit dominate the rest.
- Prefer cinematic full-bleed covers, `6/6` concept-and-art splits, four-stage gameplay rows, `7/5` world-and-audience layouts, and full-width roadmap structures.
- Use `16–22 px` between major modules and `8–13 px` within panels. Keep the density disciplined and readable at presentation distance.
- Body pages should remain consistently dark. Use key art in bounded frames so evidence and captions do not disappear into the image.

## Color system

### Core palette

- Game-interface black: `#080D13`. Use for the main canvas and deepest chart fields.
- Elevated midnight: `#121A24`. Use for cards, tables, concept panels, and production modules.
- Ember orange: `#FF6B3B`. Use for core fantasy, creative differentiation, active roadmap milestones, funding asks, and important commercial values.
- Spirit mint: `#52DFA3`. Use for core-loop completion, verified build progress, retention or quality signals, launch state, and positive evidence.
- Warm white: `#F3EDE2`. Use for headlines, primary values, and essential labels.
- Steel slate: `#7F8994`. Use for descriptions, inactive stages, benchmark context, and sources.
- Deep line: `#2B3540`. Use for panel borders, comparison rows, timelines, and chart grids.

### Semantic use

- Orange belongs to the game's fantasy, differentiator, commercial decision, or current active milestone.
- Mint communicates a functioning loop, verified progress, completed gate, or supported positive signal; it does not make a target true.
- Keep character or environment art color-faithful. Do not recolor art merely to force it into the interface palette.
- Use red only for an explicit production, financial, platform, or market risk and pair it with an owner or mitigation.

## Typography

- Use `Inter`, `IBM Plex Sans`, `Arial`, or another sturdy modern sans-serif for the interface.
- A restrained slab serif may be used only for the cover title if it matches the game's identity; otherwise stay with the sans-serif system.
- Use `IBM Plex Mono`, `Roboto Mono`, or a similar mono face for build versions, platform names, technical targets, dates, source labels, and milestone state.
- Cover title: `52–66 px`, bold. Page headline: `31–40 px`, bold. Section code: `9–11 px`, uppercase, tracked. Body: `14–17 px`. Tables and captions: `10–13 px`. Sources: `8–10 px`.
- Highlight one phrase per headline in orange or mint. Keep long text warm white or slate.
- Use tabular numerals for budget, price, units, wishlists, retention, timeline, and platform targets.

## Components

- Cards use elevated-midnight fills, `1 px` steel or colored borders, small corners, and no shadow. A thin orange or mint edge can identify creative versus validated evidence.
- Concept cards contain logline, player role, goal, obstacle, core fantasy, and one or more creative pillars.
- Gameplay stages need player action, system response, feedback, progression, expected duration, and return trigger.
- Evidence cards must label build state, metric definition, period, source, and whether the number is actual, target, forecast, or benchmark.
- Player profiles should focus on motivations, adjacent games, platforms, behavior, and purchase context, not invented biographies.
- Budget modules show discipline, owner, duration, milestone, contingency, and partner contribution.

## Charts and diagrams

- Favor loop diagrams, staged mechanics, feature comparisons, world or level maps, audience profiles, market or genre comparisons, progress cards, business-model tables, comparable-title bars, production roadmaps, team matrices, and proportional budgets.
- Gameplay diagrams should show cause and effect, feedback, failure or mastery, session rhythm, and progression—not only a list of features.
- Comparison pages must use consistent genre, platform, region, release window, price, and metric basis.
- Market views should separate total genre interest, realistically addressable audience, wishlist or community evidence, units, and revenue scenarios.
- Production roadmaps need gates such as vertical slice, alpha, content lock, beta, certification, launch, and post-launch, with acceptance criteria and dependencies.
- Avoid 3D pie charts, decorative skill trees, fake HUD gauges, and world maps that cannot explain gameplay or production scope.

## Composition families

### Cinematic pitch cover

Use one rights-cleared or project-owned hero environment across the canvas with a strong dark gradient for legibility. Place a large title and genre-platform-release line on the left, then compact team, build status, and ask details along the bottom.

### Concept and core fantasy

Pair a structured logline and three creative pillars with one representative concept frame. Add an adjacent-title or taste comparison only to clarify audience expectation and differentiation.

### Gameplay loop and differentiation

Use four or fewer loop stages, one target session or retention hypothesis, and a comparison table explaining what the project changes relative to relevant games.

### World, art direction, and audience

Use one large world image with a precise art-direction caption and three behavior-led target-player modules. Separate aesthetic affinity from evidence of demand.

### Progress and business model

Show build completion only with a defined denominator. Pair real development evidence with pricing, editions or DLC only when relevant, revenue logic, and clearly scoped comparable titles.

### Team, roadmap, budget, and ask

Use a milestone line, compact role-coverage table, proportional budget, contingency, runway, partner contribution, and a precise closing ask. Make missing capabilities visible.

## Imagery

- Use project-owned screenshots, captures, concept art, environment paintings, character sheets, UI, maps, animation frames, and production artifacts.
- Clearly label concept, target render, in-engine, gameplay capture, prototype, vertical slice, alpha, or final-quality image.
- Preserve consistent aspect ratios and a shared cinematic grade, but do not hide gameplay readability or production gaps behind atmospheric overlays.
- Use small geometric icons for loop stages and platform or production states.
- Avoid unrelated fantasy stock art, AI imagery presented as production work, mock reviews, fake store pages, generic controllers, esports imagery for noncompetitive games, and art that misrepresents the intended build.

## Content integrity

- Do not invent build completion, wishlists, followers, retention, playtest results, press, nominations, market size, genre growth, price, unit sales, revenue, platform support, team credits, budget, runway, milestones, publisher interest, or release date.
- Label every image by production status. Concept art and target renders are not gameplay evidence.
- Define build percentage by completed, accepted scope rather than intuition. Identify content, code, art, audio, design, QA, localization, certification, and platform dependencies.
- Player and market claims must state geography, platform, genre, source, period, sample, and comparison method.
- Comparable-title scenarios must account for release timing, price, discounts, refunds, platform fees, tax, regional mix, marketing, and selection bias.
- Team credits must be accurate and role-relevant. Clearly identify contractors, advisors, unfilled roles, and contingent hires.
- If evidence is missing, omit it or label it `concept`, `prototype`, `target`, `forecast`, `benchmark`, `planned`, or `to be validated`. Never invent a number or quote to complete the pitch.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview studio, title, creative fantasy, mechanics, art, players, metrics, comparables, business model, team, budget, ask, roadmap, or contact details.
- Do not let beautiful concept art substitute for playable proof, production planning, market evidence, or scope control.
- Do not describe a mechanic as unique without a defined comparison set and current implementation status.
- Do not present followers, wishlists, press, or awards as guaranteed sales.
- Do not use every panel border in orange or mint; reserve color for meaningful state and hierarchy.
- Do not use glossy gradients, glass cards, heavy glow, oversized rounded corners, 3D charts, or tiny HUD-like text.
- Do not hide platform certification, performance, accessibility, localization, content, legal, IP, community, or launch risks.
